subject: Climate & Environment
title: Cars and Carbon
description: A quick, practical guide to Cars and Carbon.

hook.text: Transport produces about 16% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Cars are the biggest share.

buildup.text: The average car sits parked 95% of the time. When it moves, it carries 1.5 people on average.

discovery.text: A single bus can replace 40 cars. A train replaces hundreds. The math is simple.

twist.text: Cities designed around cars become hostile to walking, cycling, and public life.

climax.text: The most sustainable trip is the one you never need to make — because you live near what you need.

punchline.text: We built cities for cars. Now we need cities for people.

quiz.question: What percentage of the time is the average car parked?

details.summary: Private cars are responsible for roughly 10 percent of global CO2 emissions through tailpipe exhaust and fuel production. Car-dependent cities also suffer from congestion, air pollution, and sprawl that locks in high-emission development patterns for decades.
details.whyItMatters: Reducing car dependence is essential for cutting urban emissions. Cities designed around cars face compounding climate, health, and equity challenges that grow worse over time.
takeaways: Private cars contribute about 10 percent of global CO2
Car-dependent layouts lock in decades of high emissions
Congestion and air pollution harm health and productivity

faq.question: How much CO2 does an average car emit per year?
faq.answer: A typical gasoline car driven 12,000 miles emits about 4.6 tonnes of CO2 per year. Including fuel production and vehicle manufacturing, lifecycle emissions are roughly 30 percent higher. These figures drop dramatically with electric vehicles powered by clean grids.

faq.question: Can cities really reduce car use?
faq.answer: Yes. Cities that invest in transit, cycling infrastructure, and walkable neighborhoods see significant shifts away from driving. Amsterdam, Copenhagen, and Tokyo demonstrate that dense, well-connected cities can function with far fewer private cars.
